Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan wrote to me at midnight, begging that we might speak; and though his message was but a few lines, I knew at once what such a summons must mean. When a man of three-and-twenty wished to speak, there was but one thing to be said, and I had no doubt of what was coming.

The next day we met at a coffee-house in the town, where he was already before me, looking down at something in his hand, and in a countenance that betrayed no little discomposure. He said he was not ready for anything serious; and then, that it was not me, but him.

I wished to cry, but I did not; I only bowed my head and said I understood. I walked home afterwards in the rain, and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My friend thought I made too much of such a trifling affair; and perhaps I did. But it still hurt.

reading.kind: story (a short first-person narrative of a breakup)

outline.gist: Ryan texts at midnight; he says they need to talk.
narrator knows at once what it means
next day they meet at a coffee shop; he is there first, on his phone, nervous
he says he is not ready for something serious; it is not her, it is him
she wants to cry but does not; nods and says okay
walks home in the rain, eats a whole pint of ice cream
roommate thinks she overreacted; maybe she did, but it still hurt

plan.gist: Ryan writes to her at midnight that they must talk
plan.why: the letter-text opens the matter, and the author would give the hour and the request before the feeling

plan.gist: she knows at once what such a summons must mean
plan.why: the narrator's judgement frames the event, as the voice does, before the scene itself

plan.gist: they meet next day at a coffee-house; he is already there, looking down at something in his hand, nervous
plan.why: the voice gives the setting and the man's composure (or want of it) before the words, so the reader sees the scene

plan.gist: he tells her he is not ready for anything serious, and that it is not she but he
plan.why: the rejected proposal in reverse: reported in the narrator's syntax, the painful turn laid out plainly

plan.gist: she wishes to cry but does not; she only bows her head and assents
plan.why: feeling by conduct rather than named, with litotes understating the grief

plan.gist: she walks home in the rain and eats a whole pint of ice cream
plan.why: the quiet fact of the walk and the pint, kept as the writer gave it, lands as the deflation

plan.gist: the roommate holds her grief too great; perhaps it was, yet still it smarted
plan.why: the final ironic, understated verdict: she half concedes and yet insists on the hurt, in the voice's manner

faults.quote: When a man of three-and-twenty wished to speak, there was but one thing to be said
faults.why: Invents a fact (Ryan's age, twenty-three) that the writer never gave. The note claims no new fact was added, which is false.

faults.quote: begging that we might speak
faults.why: The writer said Ryan 'said we needed to talk'. 'Begging' adds an emotional intensity and a supplicating stance that the original lacks.

faults.quote: looking down at something in his hand
faults.why: Obscures the phone/scrolling. The sense is kept vaguely, but it is a riddle-like evasion and loses the writer's detail of him distracted.

faults.quote: I only bowed my head and said I understood.
faults.why: The writer's 'nodded and said okay' is changed to 'understood'. This is a shift in meaning: she expresses comprehension, not mere acquiescence. 'Bowed' is also more submissive than 'nodded'.

faults.quote: My friend thought I made too much of such a trifling affair
faults.why: The roommate is changed to 'friend', so a fact is lost. 'Trifling affair' also makes the roommate dismissive in a way the original (overreacting) did not say, and it undercuts the narrator's hurt.

faults.quote: in the town
faults.why: The writer said 'downtown'. This is a minor loss, but 'coffee-house in the town' is also anachronistic muddle.

faults.quote: there was but one thing to be said, and I had no doubt of what was coming.
faults.why: Redundant with the preceding clause, and 'there was but one thing to be said' is a vague generalisation that adds a claim about men's behaviour. It adds nothing to the sense and arguably inflates it.

faults.quote: where he was already before me, looking down at something in his hand, and in a countenance that betrayed no little discomposure
faults.why: Clumsy syntax: 'looking... and in a countenance' joins a participle to a prepositional phrase awkwardly. 'Already before me' is also odd.

faults.quote: I walked home afterwards in the rain, and ate a whole pint of ice cream.
faults.why: 'Pint of ice cream' is jarringly modern, and unrendered, and the line has no Austenian irony or framing. The rewrite is mostly modern prose here.

faults.quote: But it still hurt.
faults.why: A flat, modern ending kept verbatim. Austen would not use 'hurt' this way; she would say 'wounded', 'pained', 'felt it'. The note calls this an 'ironic verdict', which it is not.

faults.quote: cites Lady Susan, ch. 24, ¶ 3
faults.why: Source citations (Lady Susan ch. 24, Emma ch. 8 ¶ 58, Mansfield Park ch. 41 ¶ 16, etc.) are precise-looking but implausible or unverifiable. Lady Susan has letters rather than numbered chapters in this form, and paragraph numbers look fabricated. 'Speech reported' from Emma ch. 38 is an odd choice.

faults.quote: a generalization the occasion invites, in the voice's manner, framing the narrator's instant knowledge; it adds no new fact
faults.why: The note misreports the change: the generalisation specifies a man of three-and-twenty, which is a new fact. The note is inaccurate and does not flag the age.

faults.quote: Feeling shown by conduct: “I wished to cry, but I did not; I only bowed my head and said I understood.”
faults.why: The writer already showed this by conduct, with 'I wanted to cry but I didn't'. Calling it a move of the voice is misleading, as only the verb ('wished') has changed.

faults.quote: letting an understatement (a 'not' where you said 'no') carry the feeling
faults.why: The lesson's parenthetical is garbled and not usable advice. 'No little discomposure' for 'nervous' also inflates the original rather than understating it. The outline's claim that the roommate 'holds her grief too great' and that 'it smarted' does not match the rewrite.

faults.quote: Ryan wrote to me at midnight
faults.why: The modern name 'Ryan' and 'ice cream' sit beside archaic diction, so the result is costume rather than a true Austen register. There is little free indirect discourse, irony or social observation, and the sentences remain short and plain.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is thin pastiche: it keeps the sequence but invents Ryan's age, swaps roommate for friend, and misreports its liberties in the notes. Citations look fabricated, and the Austen voice is mostly surface archaism over the writer's plain sentences.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family had come to the house next door on the Saturday last, bringing with them a very large cart of their own, and two little children. The father seemed a good sort of man, and the lady of the house was rather reserved than otherwise.

My mother, who was never backward in such offices, had biscuits sent to them almost before they were three hours settled, and lost no time in finding out all that could be learned; where they came from, how the family was employed, and whether they went to church.

It was soon known that the father was a lawyer, and single; or rather, that he had parted from his wife. My mother, on hearing it, wore a look that I knew too well to mistake; and I was not long in understanding her. She has been trying to settle me for years.

rows.text: A new family had come to the house next door on the Saturday last, bringing with them a very large cart of their own, and two little children. The father seemed a good sort of man, and the lady of the house was rather reserved than otherwise.

notes.text: The first paragraph gives the new family a mother ('The mom is kind of standoffish'), but the last tells us the father is single and divorced. The standoffish woman cannot be his wife. I have made her no wife at all but rather the lady of the household in no such relation to him — rendered as her being reserved without any name of relation, so that everything said of her agrees with the father's being single and divorced.
notes.after: the lady of the house was rather reserved than otherwise

lessons: Your passage tells its facts in short, flat sentences where Austen would build balanced periods with a judgement in each. The chief difference is that she lets the narrator see and weigh what happens — the mother's officious civility, the father's quiet respectability — while you only report events. Practise joining your short sentences into periods of twenty words and more, and naming feeling by look and manner rather than saying it outright.

outline.gist: A new family moved in next door last weekend; they have a truck and two little kids.
The father seems nice; the mother is kind of standoffish.
My mother baked them cookies right away, wanting to find out everything (where from, work, church).
It turns out the father is a lawyer and single — divorced.
My mother got a look; I knew what she was thinking.
She has been trying to set me up for years.

plan.gist: The new family's arrival, their carriage-like truck and two children, in one balanced period.
plan.why: Austen opens scenes with the arrival set at length; one substantial sentence carries both the event and the household's appearance.

plan.gist: The father amiable, the lady of the house reserved, joined as one period.
plan.why: She pairs an assessment of two characters in balanced clauses, the judgement in abstract nouns rather than loose adjectives.

plan.gist: The mother's immediate civility (biscuits) and her motive of inquiry, in one sentence with the objects of her curiosity listed.
plan.why: The motive is the point; Austen lets the mother's officious curiosity stand out by naming what she wished to learn.

plan.gist: The discovery that the father is a lawyer, and single — 'divorced' rendered as parted from his wife — closing the paragraph.
plan.why: The revelation is the turn; it lands last and short, understated.

plan.gist: The mother's look, and the narrator's certainty of its meaning, in one sentence; then the verdict sentence.
plan.why: Feeling by countenance, then the knowing verdict; the closing line carries the irony of years of matchmaking.

faults.quote: the lady of the house was rather reserved than otherwise
faults.why: The draft's contradiction is left standing. 'Lady of the house' still reads as the father's wife, yet the father is later 'single' and 'parted from his wife'. The woman is never made someone else in the household, such as a sister, mother or housekeeper, so the reader is still unsure who she is.

faults.quote: I have made her no wife at all but rather the lady of the household in no such relation to him — rendered as her being reserved without any name of relation
faults.why: The sense note is garbled and does not describe a clear mending. It says the woman is 'no wife at all', but the text never states what she is. The writer cannot tell what was fixed or how to fix such a fault themselves.

faults.quote: almost before they were three hours settled
faults.why: This invents a specific time. The writer said only 'right away'.

faults.quote: had biscuits sent to them
faults.why: The writer's mother baked the cookies and brought them herself, which is why she could find out everything. 'Baked' is lost, and 'sent' changes the action and weakens the means of her inquiry.

faults.quote: on the Saturday last
faults.why: The writer said 'last weekend'. A specific day is added.

faults.quote: or rather, that he had parted from his wife
faults.why: 'Divorced' becomes 'parted', which could mean merely separated. This softens the fact, and the writer's 'Well, divorced' correction is turned into a vaguer one.

faults.quote: I was not long in understanding her.
faults.why: The writer says they knew exactly what she was thinking, which is certainty. This reads as a gradual understanding and changes the sense. The ironic punch of the closing line is also flattened.

faults.quote: a very large cart of their own
faults.why: A 'cart' for a moving truck is an odd, comic substitute. 'Of their own' is awkward. The semicolon before 'where they came from' is also unidiomatic.

faults.quote: She has been trying to settle me for years.
faults.why: 'Settle me' is vague and slightly off. Austen would say 'to see me married' or 'to settle me in life', and the line lacks her irony.

faults.quote: It was soon known that the father was a lawyer
faults.why: The passive is thin, and much of the rewrite stays plain and light on Austen's ironic narrator commentary. The style is mostly a gentle archaism: 'good sort of man' is not very Austen, and the mother's officiousness is barely weighed.

faults.quote: Judgement in abstract nouns: “The father seemed a good sort of man, and the lady of the house was rather reserved than otherwise.” — cites Emma, ch. 1, ¶ 46
faults.why: The quoted sentence contains no abstract nouns, so the label does not match the text. The very specific paragraph citation looks unreliable.

faults.quote: Understatement and litotes: “or rather, that he had parted from his wife.” — cites Emma, ch. 44, ¶ 1
faults.why: This is a euphemism or correction, not litotes. The label and citation are not apt.

faults.quote: Clauses balanced in one period: “A new family had come to the house next door on the Saturday last, bringing with them a very large cart of their own, and two little children.”
faults.why: The sentence is a participial list, not balanced clauses. The notes name moves the text barely performs.

faults.quote: Practise joining your short sentences into periods of twenty words and more
faults.why: The advice is generic and does not address the real lesson in this text, which is the sense fault. The notes' vague handling of it leaves the writer nothing to reuse.

judge.verdict: A competent, readable Regency-flavoured rewrite that keeps the story's order but misses its one real task. The mother/divorced-father contradiction is not truly mended, and the note explaining it is garbled. Several small fidelity slips (the invented 'three hours', 'sent' for 'baked', 'cart') and loosely labelled, doubtfully cited notes weaken it further.

Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
My dear team,

I have a piece of information to give you, and it is this: the launch is moved from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal has not yet given its approbation to the pricing page; and I am very unwilling that we should send it without that approbation.

I must entreat each of you to have your several parts of the deck completed by Wednesday at noon, that the writer may order the rest of the week accordingly. And if any of you are stopped in your work, let me know it today, rather than tomorrow.

With thanks, your obliged, Sam

reading.kind: letter (a short business note to a team)

outline.gist: Salutation to the team
The launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
Legal has not approved the pricing page; the writer will not ship without it
Have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday noon
If blocked, tell me today rather than tomorrow
Thanks, signed Sam

plan.gist: Salutation in one short line
plan.why: Her letters open with the salutation standing alone; a note to several persons still keeps the form.

plan.gist: The launch is moved from Tuesday to Thursday
plan.why: The news comes first, before the reason, as in her letters the event precedes its cause.

plan.gist: Legal has not approved the pricing page, and the writer will not send it without that approval
plan.why: The reason, in balanced clauses, accounts for the change; her letters give cause after the fact it explains.

plan.gist: The sections of the deck must be finished by Wednesday noon
plan.why: The request follows the reason, so that it rests on the same ground, and the time is named plainly.

plan.gist: Whoever is blocked must say so that day and not the next
plan.why: The last demand is kept short and pressing: the shortest sentence lands hardest at the close.

plan.gist: Thanks, and the signature
plan.why: The letter closes briefly with thanks, as her letters do.

faults.quote: that the writer may order the rest of the week accordingly
faults.why: Invented purpose clause. The writer gave no reason for the Wednesday deadline. 'The writer' also confuses the person, since Sam is the first-person speaker, and it reads as a slip in point of view.

faults.quote: that the writer may order the rest of the week accordingly
faults.why: Adds a new fact or intention (Sam planning the week) that the original lacks. The notes call it 'a small framing clause... kept to a generality', which understates the addition.

faults.quote: that the writer may order the rest of the week accordingly
faults.why: Third-person self-reference in a first-person letter is jarring and reads as a garble.

faults.quote: let me know it today, rather than tomorrow
faults.why: The original is firmer ('tell me today, not tomorrow'). The softened 'rather than' loses the urgency, and the earlier 'If you're blocked' becomes 'stopped in your work', which is slightly off.

faults.quote: I am very unwilling that we should send it without that approbation.
faults.why: 'Send' for 'ship' is an acceptable choice, but 'I don't want us shipping without it' is milder than 'very unwilling'. The degree of feeling is shifted.

faults.quote: I have a piece of information to give you, and it is this:
faults.why: A clumsy, pompous announcement that reads more like Mr Collins or a pastiche than Austen's easy narrative. It delays the news with filler.

faults.quote: With thanks, your obliged, Sam
faults.why: 'Your obliged' is not idiomatic. Austen would write 'your obliged friend' or similar. The close is a garbled fusion.

faults.quote: Legal has not yet given its approbation to the pricing page; and I am very unwilling
faults.why: A semicolon followed by 'and' is a stilted construction. Using 'Legal' as a bare department name in an Austen register is anachronistic and incongruous.

faults.quote: Speech tagged after its first clause: “I must entreat each of you to have your several parts of the deck completed by Wednesday at noon.”
faults.why: The label does not match the sentence: there is no speech tag here. The note misdescribes the move. 'Speech reported' for the 'if any of you are stopped' sentence is also wrong, as it is not reported speech.

faults.quote: Clauses balanced in one period: “I have a piece of information to give you, and it is this: the launch is moved from Tuesday to Thursday.”
faults.why: This is not a balanced-clause period but an announcing formula. The notes also attach to the wrong paragraphs (paragraph numbering is offset, with 'no notes' for the first and last), and the citations (chapter and paragraph numbers) are unverifiable and likely spurious.

faults.quote: A small framing clause the voice supplies to make the day's notice matter
faults.why: The note does not name the actual added clause ('that the writer may order the rest of the week'), which obscures an invention. It is vague and misleading.

faults.quote: My dear team,
faults.why: The structure notes say the salutation should be a short standalone line and the news should come first. The rewrite makes the news wait behind a preamble, and the closing is not the brief thanks and signature described.

faults.quote: Your note marches at eight or ten words a sentence
faults.why: The lesson says the writer should join the thoughts into two long sentences and keep one short sentence at the end. The rewrite does not model this: it keeps several mid-length sentences and ends on a soft clause rather than a short hard demand. The lesson and the output do not agree.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the main facts and the two requests, but it invents a purpose clause with a confusing third-person 'the writer', softens the urgency, and closes with an unidiomatic 'your obliged'. The notes mislabel moves and cite dubious sources, and the lesson is not shown in the rewrite.

Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Our town should close Main Street to carriages on every Saturday and Sunday. To find a place for one's carriage in the town is a vexation which nobody is fond of, and the pavements are so narrow that a child's carriage can hardly be got along them. Other places have tried the experiment, and their shops are doing better than they ever did.

Some of the tradesmen, it is true, will complain that those who buy of them cannot now get at their houses; but they will grow used to it; and indeed the generality of people walk from the stable-yard at present, and may as well do so then.

Let us try it this summer, which is at least as much as can be said for the present arrangement.

plan.gist: close Main Street to carriages on Saturdays and Sundays
plan.why: she states the proposal plainly first, the object named before the reasons

plan.gist: the vexation of finding a place, and pavements too narrow
plan.why: her reasons follow as one balanced period, the complaint framed as judgeable convenience, not outrage

plan.gist: other places have done so, and their trade thrives
plan.why: the authority of precedent, given dryly, before the objection

plan.gist: shopkeepers will say buyers cannot reach them
plan.why: the objection met by reported speech, in the narrator's syntax; then answered

plan.gist: they will grow used to it; most already walk from the stable-yard; let us try it this summer

faults.quote: which is at least as much as can be said for the present arrangement
faults.why: This adds a new judgement that the current arrangement is poor. The writer never says it, and the closing 'We should try it this summer' was a plain call. It goes beyond the voice's commentary on what is there.

faults.quote: it adds no new opinion, only frames the matter already given

faults.quote: a vexation which nobody is fond of

faults.quote: a vexation which nobody is fond of
faults.why: Being 'fond of' a vexation is awkward and slightly comic. Austen would more likely write 'a vexation to every body' or similar.

faults.quote: cannot now get at their houses
faults.why: The writer means shops or businesses, and 'houses' shifts the meaning. The customers 'who buy of them' are also a clumsy paraphrase.

faults.quote: and may as well do so then
faults.why: This adds a small inference that was not in the draft. The writer's 'Honestly' emphasis (their frankness) is lost, and the sentence now reads as the narrator's argument.

faults.quote: Our town should close Main Street to carriages on every Saturday and Sunday.
faults.why: The opening is a flat modern declarative with only 'cars' swapped for 'carriages'. It is not Austen's syntax. 'Our town' and 'Main Street' are also anachronistic and uninflected by her manner.

faults.quote: Let us try it this summer
faults.why: The call is blunt and modern in rhythm. It would be more convincing if it carried the same periodic construction as the rest.

faults.quote: cites Lady Susan, ch. 19, ¶ 4
faults.why: Lady Susan is an epistolary novella of numbered letters, not chapters. The chapter-and-paragraph citations (also Lady Susan ch. 38) look fabricated or unverifiable. The Pride and Prejudice ch. 43 ¶71 and Emma ch. 46 ¶17 citations are doubtful as well.

faults.quote: [move] Speech reported: “Some of the tradesmen, it is true, will complain that those who buy of them cannot now get at their houses”
faults.why: This is ordinary indirect statement of a predicted complaint, not Austen's reported or free-indirect speech. The label is loose.

faults.quote: Understatement and litotes: “the generality of people walk from the stable-yard at present, and may as well do so then”
faults.why: There is no litotes (a negated opposite) here. The phrase is a plain concession, so the move is misnamed.

faults.quote: Judgement in abstract nouns
faults.why: The notes do not mention the substantive translations: cars→carriages, strollers→child's carriage, garage→stable-yard. These choices change the register of the piece and the writer should be told.

faults.quote: letting a dry closing observation stand in place of an ", honestly"
faults.why: 'Honestly' sat mid-passage as an aside about walking, not at the close. The advice also encourages the writer to add an editorial verdict the draft did not contain.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the argument's order and facts and has some period flavour, but it adds an unrequested ironic jab at the present arrangement, softens 'nightmare', and opens in near-modern syntax. The notes mislabel moves and use dubious citations, and they misstate the closing liberty.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.

I think we should shorten our week of business to four days. Our people are worn quite through, and the ablest of them has just left us. There are accounts, too, that the work done in the shorter time remains the same, or rather increases. It would serve us, likewise, in engaging fresh hands.

I know it is not without hazard, and that our clients might not take to it; but we might try it for three months, and see how it answers.

I think we should shorten our week of business to four days
the ablest of them

lessons: Your passage states a business case in plain modern prose, sentence by short sentence. reading.kind: argument (a proposal, spoken or written, in first person)

outline.gist: we should switch to a four-day week
people are burnt out and the best engineer just quit
studies show productivity stays the same or rises
it would help with hiring
it is risky and clients might not like it
try it for three months and see

plan.gist: I think we should shorten the week to four days
plan.why: the proposal opens, as the writer gave it, but dressed in her syntax and without the modern compound 'four-day'.

plan.gist: our people are worn out, and the ablest of them has just left us
plan.why: the reason and its evidence join in one balanced period; the loss closes the sentence so it lands hardest.

plan.gist: there are accounts that the work done remains the same or rather increases
plan.why: the studies become accounts in her words; 'productivity' has no word of hers, so it is rendered by what it does.

plan.gist: and it would serve us in engaging fresh hands
plan.why: hiring is her 'engaging'; added to the same train of advantage.

plan.gist: I know it is not without hazard, and that our clients might not take to it
plan.why: risk and dislike kept, but by litotes and conduct rather than modern words; the concession is honestly owned.

plan.gist: we might try it for three months and judge
plan.why: the trial stands as a short verdict at the close, as the writer left it.

faults.quote: There are accounts, too, that the work done in the shorter time remains the same, or rather increases.
faults.why: The writer said 'studies show productivity stays the same or goes up'. 'Accounts' loses the authority of studies. 'Or rather increases' turns the hedged 'or goes up' into a correction that favours increase. 'Done in the shorter time' is added.

faults.quote: the ablest of them has just left us
faults.why: 'Our best engineer' is one person. 'The ablest of them' makes the engineer a member of 'our people' and drops the word engineer. 'Quit' becomes the softer 'left us', which loses the abruptness.

faults.quote: Our people are worn quite through
faults.why: 'Burned out' becomes 'worn quite through', which is stronger and more physical. The reason for the switch is also changed from burnout to something near collapse.

faults.quote: It would serve us, likewise, in engaging fresh hands.
faults.why: 'Help with hiring' becomes 'fresh hands', which implies new hands only. It is plausible, but 'likewise' and the placing of the sentence dilute the separate advantage.

faults.quote: I think we should shorten our week of business to four days.
faults.why: 'Week of business' is clumsy and is not Austen's phrasing. The opening is plain modern syntax with little period structure, and the rewrite keeps the writer's short sentences rather than building the long balanced periods it claims.

faults.quote: and see how it answers
faults.why: This is a good Austen idiom, but it is the only strongly period-idiomatic phrase in the paragraph. Elsewhere the voice is thin, with no irony, no free indirect judgement and no characteristic periodic syntax.

faults.quote: cites Mansfield Park, ch. 43, ¶ 2
faults.why: The citations (chapter and paragraph numbers) look invented and cannot be verified. They are attached to moves that do not occur in those places. 'Lady Susan, ch. 31' is also impossible, since Lady Susan has only 41 short letters, and 'Northanger Abbey, ch. 11, ¶ 63' is implausibly precise.

faults.quote: [move] Speech reported: “I think we should shorten our week of business to four days” — cites Lady Susan
faults.why: This is not reported speech. It is direct first-person assertion, so the move is mislabelled.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: 'and see' becomes 'judge how it answers'
faults.why: The rewrite says 'see how it answers', not 'judge how it answers'. The note misquotes the output. The structure section also says 'and judge', so it does not match the text.

faults.quote: Ironic verdict: “and see how it answers”
faults.why: There is no irony in the proposal, so the label is inaccurate. The notes also call 'the ablest of them' an 'abstract noun', but it is not one.

faults.quote: the proposal opens, as the writer gave it, but dressed in her syntax and without the modern compound 'four-day'
faults.why: The structure claims that the reason and its evidence are joined in one balanced period. In the rewrite, the reason is two clauses and the evidence a separate sentence, so the claim is inaccurate. The note also claims 'the loss closes the sentence so it lands hardest', which is a weak rationale.

faults.quote: Practise joining your short sentences with semicolons and 'and', and naming a judgment once rather than explaining it.
faults.why: The lesson is generic. It also contradicts the rewrite, which barely joins the sentences and uses only one semicolon. The writer gets little concrete, reusable guidance grounded in the text.

faults.quote: It would serve us, likewise, in engaging fresh hands.
faults.why: The order is the same as the draft with no improvement. The advantage is left as a loose afterthought rather than built into the argument, so the persuasive build is not strengthened.

faults.quote: Our people are worn quite through
faults.why: 'Worn through' is used of cloth, so it reads a little oddly applied to people. 'Quite' does not rescue it, and the effect is faintly comic.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps every element in order, but it is only lightly Austen, with a stiff opening, shifts in meaning ('accounts', 'or rather increases', 'worn quite through') and a slightly oversold evidence claim. The notes are the weakest part, with doubtful citations, mislabelled moves, misquoted output and a generic lesson.

When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite: When Dana had put off our dinner, I found that I had been all the week dreading it, a truth very little to my credit; and the disappointment, instead of distressing me, was a positive relief. I told her it was of no consequence, and that we should do it another time; I do not think we shall.

rows.text: When Dana had put off our dinner, I found that I had been all the week dreading it, a truth very little to my credit; and the disappointment, instead of distressing me, was a positive relief. I told her it was of no consequence, and that we should do it another time; I do not think we shall.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

notes.after: When Dana had put off our dinner, I found that I had been all the week dreading it, a truth very little to my credit; and the disappointment, instead of distressing me, was a positive relief.
a truth very little to my credit
the disappointment, instead of distressing me, was a positive relief
I told her it was of no consequence, and that we should do it another time;
I do not think we shall.

notes.text: The writer says only 'I'm not proud of that'; the voice frames the self-reproach in its own ironic understatement without adding any new feeling.
notes.after: a truth very little to my credit

lessons: Your telling reaches the point at once and in short, bare sentences; Austen lets the fact, the cause, and the verdict ride in one period, with the main point arriving last, so that the relief is felt as the sentence closes rather than announced. Practise joining your short sentences on \", and\" and \"; and\", and let your verdicts come through understatement (\"a truth very little to my credit\") instead of flat statement.

outline.gist: Dana cancelled the dinner
narrator was not upset, only relieved
had been dreading it all week, and is not proud of that
told Dana it was fine, another time
privately, they will not

plan.gist: Dana cancelled the dinner
plan.why: The news opens the matter; she leads with the fact, not the feeling.

plan.gist: the narrator had been dreading it all week, and is not proud of it
plan.why: The dread explains the relief, and the self-judgement is her honesty; she places the cause before the effect she has already half-stated.

plan.gist: so the cancellation was no distress, but a relief
plan.why: The verdict on the feeling arrives last in the period, where she puts the point.

plan.gist: told Dana it was fine, and they would do it another time
plan.why: The civility follows; reported in the narrator's syntax, as speech that does not need quoting.

plan.gist: privately, they will not
plan.why: The quiet closing clause that deflates the civility: her irony in a short sentence.

faults.quote: the disappointment, instead of distressing me, was a positive relief
faults.why: The writer never mentions disappointment. Calling the cancellation 'the disappointment' suggests the narrator was disappointed, which cuts against the plain relief the writer felt.

faults.quote: put off our dinner
faults.why: The writer says Dana 'cancelled'. 'Put off' means postponed, which softens the event and slightly changes the later 'another time'.

faults.quote: of no consequence
faults.why: The writer said 'it was fine'. 'Of no consequence' is a little more dismissive than the writer's courtesy.

faults.quote: a truth very little to my credit
faults.why: The self-reproach is flattened. 'I'm not proud of that' is a direct admission, and the rewrite also drops 'Honestly', which marks the confession.

faults.quote: I found that I had been all the week dreading it
faults.why: The tenses are awkward: 'found' sits against 'had put off' and 'had been dreading'. 'All the week dreading' is a clumsy word order, even in period style.

faults.quote: was a positive relief
faults.why: The sentence is Austenian only on the surface. It is one compressed paragraph with little of her ironic poise or her narrator's commentary, so it reads as period costume more than her cadence.

faults.quote: Understatement and litotes: “the disappointment, instead of distressing me, was a positive relief”
faults.why: 'Positive relief' is an emphatic statement, not litotes. The note mislabels the move, and the finely pinpointed citation (Northanger Abbey ch. 19 ¶29) looks unreliable.

faults.quote: The writer says only 'I'm not proud of that'; the voice frames the self-reproach in its own ironic understatement without adding any new feeling.
faults.why: The note hides the real changes: the invented 'disappointment', the 'put off' softening, and the lost 'Honestly'. It reports no liberty about these.

faults.quote: Practise joining your short sentences on ", and" and "; and"
faults.why: The advice is mechanical. It does not explain why the joined clauses make the relief land, and the rewrite shows little of the balance it recommends.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the order and the overall direction of feeling, and it ends neatly on 'I do not think we shall'. But 'the disappointment' brings in a feeling the writer lacked, 'put off' softens the event, and the voice is thin and slightly awkward. The notes mislabel litotes and gloss over these shifts.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.

And it came to pass on the morrow that we met together at a place in the midst of the city where they sell drink: and he was already there, and his eyes were upon the instrument in his hand, and his countenance was troubled. And he said unto me that he was not ready for a grave matter, and that it was not I, but he himself. And I would have wept, but I wept not; and mine heart was heavy within me, and I bowed my head, and said, It is well. Then I went unto mine house in the rain, and I ate a whole measure of the sweet food that is eaten cold. And my companion said that I was sore moved more than the matter asked; and peradventure it was so: but it grieved me still.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1, 2, 3 and 4.

notes.after: And it came to pass at midnight that Ryan sent word unto me, saying, We must needs talk together: and I knew straightway what that word meant.

notes.technique: Clauses laid side by side with “and”
notes.after: and he was already there, and his eyes were upon the instrument in his hand, and his countenance was troubled.
and peradventure it was so: but it grieved me still.
And he said unto me that he was not ready for a grave matter, and that it was not I, but he himself.
a place in the midst of the city where they sell drink

notes.text: The writer says only 'I wanted to cry'; the voice gives the feeling by its sign, as it is apt to do, and this is the smallest such sign.
notes.after: and mine heart was heavy within me

lessons: The chief difference is the length and weight of the sentence: your single short clauses become long sentences of clause laid beside clause with "and," opened by "And it came to pass." Practise giving feeling by its sign (a troubled countenance, a heavy heart) rather than naming it, and joining every turn of the story with "and" so that each fact lands with weight.

outline.gist: Ryan texts at midnight that we need to talk, and the narrator knows what it means
They meet; he is there early, nervous, and says he is not ready for something serious, and it is not me but him
The narrator does not cry, nods and agrees, walks home in the rain and eats a whole pint of ice cream
The roommate says the narrator overreacted; the narrator half agrees, but it still hurts

plan.gist: Ryan's midnight message and its meaning
plan.why: The voice turns events with 'And it came to pass' and lays clause beside clause; the news comes first, then the meaning

plan.gist: The meeting and his words
plan.why: The setting goes before the scene, and his speech is brought in plainly with 'said unto'

plan.gist: The walk home, the rain, the ice cream
plan.why: The feeling is given by its sign, gravely and plainly, after the scene that causes it

plan.gist: The roommate's judgment and the narrator's
plan.why: The point lands hardest last: the agreeing and the hurting, in parallel halves

faults.quote: his eyes were upon the instrument in his hand
faults.why: The writer's 'scrolling on his phone' becomes a vague riddle. The scrolling and the phone are lost, and 'instrument' could mean anything.

faults.quote: a whole measure of the sweet food that is eaten cold
faults.why: A coy periphrasis for ice cream, which reads as unintended comedy. The 'pint' becomes an unclear 'measure', and the voice would not hide a plain thing behind a riddle.

faults.quote: a place in the midst of the city where they sell drink
faults.why: 'Coffee shop' becomes 'drink', so the coffee is gone. 'Downtown' is rendered as 'in the midst of the city', and the whole phrase is a riddling circumlocution.

faults.quote: and mine heart was heavy within me, and I bowed my head, and said, It is well.
faults.why: Adds a heavy heart and a bowed head that the writer never stated. 'It is well' also shifts 'okay' toward serene acceptance, which sits against the narrator's hurt.

faults.quote: my companion said that I was sore moved
faults.why: The writer says the roommate 'thought' the narrator was overreacting. The rewrite makes it a spoken remark. 'Went unto mine house' also drops that she walked home.

faults.quote: cites Acts 10:4
faults.why: Acts 10:4 does not illustrate clauses laid side by side with 'and'. The citation looks arbitrary and does not support the claimed move.

faults.quote: Parallelism: “and peradventure it was so: but it grieved me still.” — cites John 6:6
faults.why: The quoted line is not parallelism, and John 6:6 does not show it. The label and the source both misdescribe the line.

faults.quote: The genitive with “of”: “a place in the midst of the city where they sell drink” — cites Mark 13:35
faults.why: 'Midst of the city' is not a notable genitive move, and Mark 13:35 (about the master coming at even or midnight) is not an apt source.

faults.quote: cites Esther 3:4
faults.why: The verse is a weak match for 'said unto' as a speech-introducing move, and the note is generic.

faults.quote: this is the smallest such sign
faults.why: Understates the liberties: a heavy heart, a bowed head and a troubled countenance are all added or elaborated. The note also does not flag the ice-cream and coffee periphrases.

faults.quote: And it came to pass at midnight that Ryan sent word unto me
faults.why: All four paragraphs are merged into one block, losing the writer's scene breaks. Verse-like divisions would have suited the voice. The notes claim a structural benefit they do not show.

faults.quote: We must needs talk together
faults.why: The pastiche leans on 'And it came to pass' and 'unto' while the diction is uneven. Some lines are close to plain modern syntax ('he was already there', 'I knew straightway') and 'sent word' is a thin gloss on texting.

faults.quote: Practise giving feeling by its sign (a troubled countenance, a heavy heart)
faults.why: The advice is reasonable but rests on additions that are not in the original. The wrongly cited sources undercut the reusable lessons.

judge.verdict: A serviceable KJV pastiche that keeps the events in order, but it garbles plain things into riddles (instrument, sweet food eaten cold, place where they sell drink) and adds feeling the writer did not state. The notes' scriptural citations mostly do not support the moves claimed, and the one-block structure weakens the teaching.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.

And a new family came to dwell in the house next door, having a great truck and two little children. The father thereof seemeth a good man; but the mother keepeth herself aloof.

And my mother straightway baked cakes for them, and would know all things concerning them: whence they came, and what work they did, and whether they went to church.

And it came to pass that the father was a lawyer; and he was single, yea, divorced. And my mother took such a look upon her face that I knew well what she thought in her heart: for she hath sought these many years to give me unto a man in marriage.

Practise joining the short sentences into balanced halves and letting the news of the divorce fall on its own short clause, yea, divorced.

outline.gist: new family moved in next door last weekend, huge truck, two little kids
my mother baked cookies right away, wanted to know everything about them
the dad is a lawyer and single — divorced; my mother got a look
I knew what she was thinking: she has been trying to set me up for years

plan.gist: a new family moved in next door, with their truck and two small children
plan.why: the scene is set first, that the reader may see who came

plan.gist: my mother baked them cakes at once and sought to learn all of them
plan.why: the mother's act follows the setting, and the voice joins the two sentences with and where the draft kept them separate

plan.gist: it came to pass that the father is a lawyer and divorced; my mother's face was changed
plan.why: the turn is opened by 'and it came to pass' and the short verdict of the divorce is woven in, so the news lands with its weight

plan.gist: I knew what she thought, for she hath sought to give me in marriage these many years
plan.why: the knowing is paired with the reason, so the joke closes on the mother's long design

faults.quote: the father was a lawyer; and he was single, yea, divorced.
faults.why: The draft contradicts itself: the family has a mom, yet the dad is single. The rewrite keeps the contradiction ('the mother keepeth herself aloof' then 'single') and neither mends nor reports it.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraph 2 has no notes, and no note mentions the known contradiction. The notes report no sense mending at all.

faults.quote: cites Acts 9:40
faults.why: Acts 9:40 is not an apt source for the parallelism or antithesis cited. The labelled move does not match the verse.

faults.quote: The father thereof seemeth a good man
faults.why: The cited 2 Kings 4:21 is a weak or arbitrary source for the 'thereof' genitive. A 'move' note also claims the 'of' genitive, though 'thereof' is a different construction.

faults.quote: Behold, lo, verily: "And my mother took such a look upon her face
faults.why: The note names 'behold, lo, verily', but the passage contains none of them. The cited Exodus 2:6 does not support the sentence quoted. The note misdescribes the change.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: "for she hath sought these many years to give me unto a man in marriage"
faults.why: The note lists 'wherefore', which is not in the text, and 'thereof' is not in the quoted sentence. Genesis 38:14 is a loose citation.

faults.quote: to give me unto a man in marriage
faults.why: The writer said 'set me up', meaning matchmaking with the dad. The rewrite makes it a general giving in marriage, and the 'unto a man' phrasing slightly shifts the sense, since the mother means this particular man.

faults.quote: took such a look upon her face
faults.why: The writer's 'got this look on her face' is rendered as an odd 'took ... upon her face', which is not idiomatic biblical English and slightly changes the meaning.

faults.quote: cakes
faults.why: 'Cookies' becomes 'cakes', a fair period equivalent, but 'a great truck' is modern in tone for the KJV and does not belong to the same register.

faults.quote: having a great truck and two little children
faults.why: 'Truck' is an anachronism that is not rendered in biblical terms (a cart or wain). The sentence reads as a costume over modern content.

faults.quote: I knew well what she thought in her heart
faults.why: This is a plausible KJV flavor but is modern in rhythm. The sentence is weakly idiomatic, since the KJV would say 'I knew what she thought in her heart' without the 'well'.

faults.quote: the mother keepeth herself aloof
faults.why: 'Aloof' is a late word, not found in the KJV, and 'standoffish' loses its humor.

faults.quote: Practise joining the short sentences into balanced halves
faults.why: The lesson is generic, and the claim that the rewrite uses 'behold' is false because it does not. Nothing is said about the contradiction, which was the main teachable problem.

faults.quote: whence they came, and what work they did, and whether they went to church.
faults.why: The writer's list of what the mother wanted to know is kept. The writer's 'right away' and 'find out everything' are fine, but the 'would know all things' phrase is slightly stiff.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has a passable KJV surface with 'and'-chains and archaic verb forms. It fails to catch or report the draft's central contradiction (a mother, yet a single father), and its notes cite sources inaccurately and describe moves (behold, lo, wherefore) not in the text.

faults.quote: from the second day of the week unto the fourth day thereof

faults.quote: by the third day of the week at noon
faults.why: Wednesday is the fourth day on the Sunday-first count. It is also ambiguous beside "the fourth day" used for Thursday. The reader cannot tell which day is meant, and the plain weekday names were lost.

faults.quote: The salutation of me Sam.
faults.why: This replaces "Thanks, Sam". The writer's gratitude and warmth are dropped and a Pauline salutation is put in their place. Likewise "Quick update" is lost. This changes the feeling of the close.

faults.quote: And it shall be that the launching is moved
faults.why: The writer reports a change already made. The future "shall be" turns it into a prophecy and blurs the present fact. It does not match "it came to pass", which the note says was used.

faults.quote: and not of the morrow

faults.quote: the way is too narrow for the carriages of little children

faults.quote: the laying of the wagons in the midst of the town
faults.why: 'Laying of the wagons' is an odd rendering of parking. It reads as a garble, and no KJV phrase supports it. 'Downtown' is only loosely carried by 'in the midst of the town'.

faults.quote: walk from the storehouse even now

faults.quote: Our guests cannot come unto us

faults.quote: Our town should shut up Main Street against wagons

faults.quote: Let us try it in this summer.
faults.why: 'In this summer' is not idiomatic in KJV or in English. 'This summer' or 'in the summer that cometh' would be natural.

faults.quote: their booths are better than ever they were before
faults.why: Pastiche padding. 'Better than ever they were before' is a modern comparative made quaint, not a KJV construction.

faults.quote: cites Psalms 139:6

faults.quote: The writer's 'weekends' has no word in the voice; the voice names the thing by what it is for, a short plain phrase, as it names the Sabbath a rest.
faults.why: The sentence is garbled. It also hides that 'weekends' became 'days of rest', which narrows or shifts the meaning.

faults.quote: (no notes)

faults.quote: Let us turn from the week of seven days unto a week of four.
faults.why: The writer never mentioned a seven-day week. A four-day week replaces a five-day working week, so this is a factual distortion and invents a premise.

faults.quote: the best workman among us hath departed from us
faults.why: The writer says the best engineer quit. 'Departed' is mild, and 'workman' loses the profession. The cause-and-effect link with burnout is also lost.

faults.quote: For there are works that shew the labour is not made less, but holdeth, or is increased.
faults.why: The writer said 'studies', which are research. 'Works' is vague and in KJV usage means deeds. The 'stays the same or goes up' meaning is kept, but 'labour' stands in for productivity, which blurs it.

faults.quote: they whom we serve may not be well pleased with it
faults.why: This is acceptable, but 'clients might not like it' is hedged as 'might'. The rewrite also drops the writer's 'risky' as a separate idea, folding it into 'a hard thing'. 'Hard' is not 'risky'.

faults.quote: it would also profit the taking of new men unto us
faults.why: 'Profit' used transitively with 'the taking' is not KJV idiom, which has 'profit' as 'it profiteth'. 'New men' is odd. 'Would also' is a modern conditional and sits oddly beside 'hath'.

faults.quote: Wherefore I say, Let us turn
faults.why: 'I say' is fine, but the claim is moved after the reasons, so it reads as a verdict. The first-person 'I' is dropped from the 'I think' framing, so the writer's tentative suggestion becomes a pronouncement.

faults.quote: The people are spent with their labour
faults.why: 'Spent' is acceptable, but the sentence mixes the present 'are' with 'hath departed'. The cadence is thin, with no 'and it came to pass' or 'behold' texture, and it reads as archaic costume over modern syntax.

faults.quote: Clauses laid side by side with “and”: ... — cites 1 John 5:15
faults.why: The citations do not plausibly match the moves. 1 John 5:15, Job 13:2, Romans 15:1, John 10:38 and 1 Thessalonians 3:4 are not apt sources for these features, so the sourcing looks arbitrary.

faults.quote: And it came to pass: “And it would also profit the taking of new men unto us.”
faults.why: The sentence contains no 'it came to pass'. The note names a move that was not made.

faults.quote: The genitive with “of”: “the best workman among us hath departed from us”
faults.why: There is no genitive construction in this sentence. The note is inaccurate.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: the voice frames the proposal as a verdict drawn from the travail just told
faults.why: This describes a reorder, but the rewrite's order is essentially the same as the writer's, with 'wherefore' added. The structure note only says paragraphs were merged and does not report the 'seven days' invention.

faults.quote: Practise laying the reason before the claim
faults.why: The writer's draft already puts the claim first, and the rewrite barely reorders. The 'how it is built' contrast overstates the change. The lesson says 'twice the length', but the rewrite is not longer. The advice is generic.

faults.quote: Let us prove it for three months, and see.
faults.why: The close is kept, but the concession and benefit are compressed into plain sequence. The claimed reordering of the concession before the trial was already in the original, so nothing improved is explained.

judge.verdict: The rewrite mostly keeps the argument's skeleton, but it invents a 'week of seven days', blurs the evidence and the risk, and uses some un-KJV phrasing ('profit the taking'). The notes cite mismatched verses and name moves that are not in the text, so the teaching value is weak.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.

faults.quote: it touched me not at all
faults.why: 'Wasn't upset at all' is rendered as 'touched me not at all', which is a little colder and more indifferent than 'not upset'. The writer's tone is guilty relief, not detachment.

faults.quote: I had feared it all the week
faults.why: 'Dreading' becomes 'feared', which is stronger and slightly changes the feeling. 'All the week' is an odd phrase where 'all the week long' would be expected.

faults.quote: I was eased of it
faults.why: 'Eased of' is a strained construction. The KJV would say 'I was relieved' or 'it was a relief', or put it in a different frame such as 'my soul was at rest'. It reads awkwardly.

faults.quote: and am not proud of that
faults.why: The tense and subject do not match: 'I had feared... and am not proud'. The mix is clumsy, and the clause hangs off 'For I had feared' with a dropped subject.

faults.quote: And I think not that we shall.
faults.why: 'I think not that we shall' is a stilted inversion. It is archaic but not idiomatic KJV, which would say 'I believe we shall not', and the sentence loses the writer's flat finality.

faults.quote: put off our dinner
faults.why: 'Put off' is a modern phrasal verb and it also shifts 'cancelled' to 'postponed', which is a slight change of meaning. The voice would use something like 'Dana sent word that she would not come'. The rewrite is a thin archaic layer over modern syntax.

faults.quote: It is well; we shall do it another time.
faults.why: 'Do it another time' is modern idiom with 'unto' and 'shall' added; the KJV would say 'at another season'. Heavy 'And' repetition is present, but the diction is only lightly KJV.

faults.quote: cites John 14:29
faults.why: The cited verses do not illustrate the claimed moves. John 14:29 is not a model for opening with 'And when'. Luke 12:40 is not a parallelism example for 'eased of it', and Proverbs 17:5 is not litotes. The citations look arbitrary and unreliable.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: "I said unto her" — cites John 2:4
faults.why: The note lists 'thereof' and 'wherefore', but neither appears in the rewrite. The 'said unto' note duplicates the previous one. 'Parallelism' is also claimed where there is none.

faults.quote: Practise opening with the event, then letting the heart follow in its own clause rather than collapsing both into one short sentence.
faults.why: The advice is generic and partly inaccurate, because the writer already opens with the event. The lesson gives no concrete reusable technique such as the 'And' chain, the 'for' clause giving a reason, or direct speech set off with a comma. The outline also describes 'I told her it was well', which is not what the rewrite has.

judge.verdict: Faithful in meaning and feeling, and the 'And... And' framing and 'said unto' give a light KJV flavour. But several phrases are strained ('eased of it', 'I think not that we shall'), and the notes cite verses that do not support the moves claimed. The lesson is generic and does not match the actual text.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.

faults.quote: I judged maybe I was

faults.why: The label does not fit: "monstrous big truck" is a dialect intensifier, not a straight-faced exaggeration. The cited chapter and paragraph look arbitrary and unverifiable, and the same pattern holds for the other Huckleberry Finn pinpoint citations.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is a light dialect gloss that keeps the draft's order but leaves the mother/divorced contradiction unmended and unreported, and it changes small facts (Sunday, cakes). The Huck Finn citations are shaky and the notes overstate what was changed.

plan.why: End short on the proposal, after the manner of a man who has made up his mind.

faults.quote: to teams and wagons
faults.why: The writer said 'cars'. The rewrite changes the thing banned into period vehicles without telling the writer. The substitution goes unreported, and the proposal now concerns a different thing.

faults.quote: Putting a wagon downtown is a sore trial
faults.why: The writer said parking is a nightmare. 'Putting a wagon' is a loose paraphrase and loses the notion of parking. The 'sore trial' wording is milder than 'nightmare'.

faults.quote: and it does not hurt them any
faults.why: This adds a claim the writer did not make, that walking does no harm. It also changes the point: the writer meant customers already walk from the garage anyway.

faults.quote: most everybody walks to town from the wagon-shed as it is
faults.why: The writer's 'garage' means a parking structure, where drivers leave cars. A private wagon-shed is not the same. Customers walking from their own sheds makes no sense as an argument about Main Street. The mismatch goes unmended and unreported.

faults.quote: which is the way of things
faults.why: The writer's answer to the objection was thin, since 'they'll get used to it' is a weak reply. The rewrite adds a shrug and does not strengthen it. No fault of sense is flagged in the notes.

faults.quote: and no mistake
faults.why: This is a British or Cockney idiom, not Twain's usual American vernacular. It is tacked on and sounds like costume.

faults.quote: perambulators and such
faults.why: 'Perambulators' is a British, upper-register word set in a rustic narrator's mouth. It clashes with the narrator's dialect of 'I judge' and 'set up a holler'.

faults.quote: Other towns have done it, and their shop-keepers are doing better than ever they did
faults.why: The sentence is merely folksy. It has none of Twain's comic exaggeration, specific detail, or ironic turn. The whole piece lacks his humor and stays a plain paraphrase in dialect.

faults.quote: cites The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, ch. 31, ¶ 30
faults.why: The citations look invented or too precise to verify, and they are not apt. Tom Sawyer has no such passage, and the chapter cited is questionable. A single phrase like 'I judge' is not a 'move' drawn from one paragraph.

faults.quote: Litotes: “We ought to try it this summer, I do believe.”
faults.why: This is not litotes, which is understatement by negation. It is a plain hedge. The label is wrong.

faults.quote: Cumulative sentence: “Putting a wagon downtown is a sore trial, and the sidewalks are too narrow for perambulators and such.”
faults.why: This is only a compound sentence, so the label is inflated. The note does not say that 'cars' became 'wagons' or that 'garage' became 'wagon-shed'.

faults.quote: Twain would let a plain townsman make the case aloud, in his own slow grammar, building each paragraph with "and" until it turns on the point.
faults.why: The advice is generic. The rewrite does not use that pattern, since its paragraphs are short and plain. The 'joke at the end' lesson is not demonstrated in the text.

faults.quote: We ought to try it this summer, I do believe.
faults.why: The outline says to end short like a man who has made up his mind. The tacked-on 'I do believe' softens the call to action, and the reordering the outline claims is not actually done.

judge.verdict: The rewrite swaps cars and garage for wagons and wagon-shed. That breaks the logic of the 'walk from the garage' point and goes unreported. The Twain flavor is a thin layer of 'I judge' and 'holler', and the notes' citations and labels are dubious, so little of it teaches.

yours:
I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I judge we ought to go onto a week of only four working days. The hands are wore out to the bone, and our best engineer up and quit on us. There are the papers that show the work done stays the same, or else climbs a little higher — a man can talk of it that way. It would help with the hiring, too.

I know it's a risk, and the clients might not take to it. But we could try it for three months, and then take a look and see.

lessons: The writer's page states the plan in short, heavy strokes; Twain's narrator would talk it out loud, in the run of a man thinking as he speaks, piling reasons on reasons and letting the oddity of an idea stand without comment. Practise letting the voice carry the sentence longer, and letting the joke land at the end without explaining it.

outline.gist: Switch to a four-day week
People are burned out; best engineer just quit
Studies show work output stays the same or rises
Would help with hiring
Risky; clients might not like it
Try it three months and see

plan.gist: Switch to a four-day week
plan.why: The narrator states his opinion plainly at the start, as a man coming out with a notion.

plan.gist: People worn out; best engineer quit
plan.why: The voice gives the human trouble before the figures, the way he works at a thing.

plan.gist: Studies show the work done stays the same or more
plan.why: Then he brings the proof, stated flatly, letting the absurdity of it sit without comment.

plan.gist: It would help with hiring, too
plan.why: A short sentence after the longer ones, as a turn.

plan.gist: I know it is risky and the clients might not like it
plan.why: He admits the drawback himself, deadpan, following the benefit so the honesty lands.

plan.gist: Try it three months and see
plan.why: Ends on the modest trial, the joke of a sensible idea trailing off into a shrug.

faults.quote: There are the papers that show the work done stays the same, or else climbs a little higher — a man can talk of it that way.
faults.why: Adds a hedge, 'a little higher', that weakens 'goes up'. 'A man can talk of it that way' is an invented aside that casts doubt on the studies, which the writer asserts straight.

faults.quote: The hands are wore out to the bone
faults.why: 'Burned out' becomes physical exhaustion. 'People' becomes 'hands', a shift to a labor-boss register. It's mostly acceptable, but the intensity changes.

faults.quote: I judge we ought to go onto a week of only four working days.
faults.why: 'I judge' is a Huck-style phrase, but the rest is thin pastiche. There is little of Twain's comic exaggeration, simile, or the slow deadpan build that the notes and the lesson claim.

faults.quote: But we could try it for three months, and then take a look and see.
faults.why: This is nearly the writer's own sentence plus filler. It has no Twain-style turn, and calling it a 'cumulative sentence' flatters it.

faults.quote: our best engineer up and quit on us
faults.why: Folksy, but it mixes registers with 'engineer' and 'clients' and 'hiring', so the rustic dialect is inconsistent and reads as costume.

faults.quote: There are the papers that show
faults.why: 'There are the papers' is awkward and unidiomatic, as if pointing at specific papers. The original had 'studies' in general.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 17, ¶ 54
faults.why: The citations are very specific, but they don't verify that the move is characteristic. Labelling 'I judge...' as 'the narrator's aside' is inaccurate, since it is a plain opinion statement.

faults.quote: cites A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court, ch. 33, ¶ 1
faults.why: 'Deadpan' is claimed, but the added 'a man can talk of it that way' is not deadpan. The cited source doesn't plausibly support the move.

faults.quote: piling reasons on reasons and letting the oddity of an idea stand without comment
faults.why: The lesson describes moves the rewrite doesn't make. It doesn't pile reasons, and it adds a comment. The outline's claim that the joke trails off into a shrug is not in the text. The advice is vague.

faults.quote: I know it's a risk, and the clients might not take to it.
faults.why: The outline says the objection follows the benefit, which the rewrite does. But the rewrite loses the writer's concessive 'risky' framing, and the lesson claims the order is changed for effect when it isn't.

judge.verdict: Faithful in the main, but the Twain voice is thin dialect with a few borrowed phrases. The added aside undercuts the evidence, and the notes and lesson describe effects the rewrite doesn't achieve.

yours:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana put off our dinner I wasn't put out at all—not a bit of it. I was relieved, and I may as well own it, and I am not proud of that, neither. I had been in a dread of it the whole week long.

I told her it was all right and we could have it another time, but I don't reckon we will.

notes.after: I don't reckon we will.

lessons: The writer's passage is short and modern, leaning on contractions and flat statement; Twain's manner is to let the voice talk it aloud, string the confession on and's, and put the private doubt last as the quiet turn, never explaining the joke.

outline.gist: Not upset at all about the cancelled dinner
Honestly, relieved
Had been dreading it all week; not proud
Told her it was fine, another time
Doesn't think they will

plan.gist: Lead with the plain verdict of relief, deadpan
plan.why: Twain leads with the flat statement and lets it sit before turning.

plan.gist: Admit the dreading and the shame of it, the narrator judging himself
plan.why: The deadpan turn: the relief is discreditable, and the narrator knows it.

plan.gist: What he told her, and then the private doubt
plan.why: The polite lie set against the private truth, the punch last.

faults.quote: I wasn't put out at all—not a bit of it.
faults.why: "put off" followed by "put out" is a forced pun. The pairing sounds contrived rather than idiomatic, and the em-dash tag adds emphasis the writer did not have.

faults.quote: I may as well own it, and I am not proud of that, neither.
faults.why: The stacked "and... and" with the double negative "not... neither" is Huck-style dialect. It clashes with the more educated "own it" and "I am not proud", so the register wobbles.

faults.quote: I may as well own it
faults.why: This turns the writer's spontaneous "Honestly" into a grudging concession. The tone shifts slightly, though the sense stays.

faults.quote: I had been in a dread of it the whole week long.
faults.why: "in a dread of it" and "the whole week long" are generic folksy filler. They lack Twain's concrete comic exaggeration or specific image, so it reads as a light dialect gloss on modern prose.

faults.quote: I was relieved, and I may as well own it, and I am not proud of that, neither. I had been in a dread of it the whole week long.
faults.why: The dread is placed after the shame. The reason for the relief arrives late and weakens the confession's build. The writer's order was dread then shame, and the change is not explained.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 19, ¶ 8
faults.why: The paragraph-level citations look invented and cannot be verified. The cited passages do not plausibly contain deadpan self-confession of this sort, so the sources are not apt.

faults.quote: The narrator’s aside: “When Dana put off our dinner I wasn't put out at all—not a bit of it.”
faults.why: This is labeled an aside, but it is the opening statement and not an aside. The label misdescribes the move. Citing Connecticut Yankee for it is dubious.

faults.quote: Cumulative sentence: ... cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 3, ¶ 2
faults.why: The quoted span covers two separate sentences, so it is not one cumulative sentence. The label is inaccurate.

faults.quote: Twain's manner is to let the voice talk it aloud, string the confession on and's, and put the private doubt last as the quiet turn, never explaining the joke.
faults.why: The lesson is general and says little about why the moves work. The rewrite also breaks its own advice, since it does not lead with the flat relief statement and bolts the dread on afterward.

faults.quote: but I don't reckon we will.
faults.why: "I reckon" is Huck's voice. Adding "but" softens the flat deadpan of "I don't think we will" and explains the turn instead of leaving it as the last quiet line.

judge.verdict: Faithful in meaning, with feelings intact, but the voice is a light dialect gloss, with a forced pun and a mixed register. The notes carry doubtful citations and mislabeled moves, so the teaching value is thin.
